neunzehn.et: From Middle High German niunzëhen, from Old High German niunzehan, from Proto-Germanic *newuntehun. Equivalent to neun + zehn. Compare Dutch negentien, English nineteen, Danish nitten.

neunzig.et: From Middle High German niunzec, from Old High German niunzug, from Proto-West Germanic *neun tigiwi. Equivalent to neun + -zig.

neunschwänzige Katze.et: From an adjective composed of neun (“nine”) + Schwanz (“tail”) + -ig (“-y”), and Katze (“cat”).

s:
Martin Luther, trans., Bible, Gospel of Luke 17:17,
„Wo sind aber die neune?“
neun.et: From Old High German niun, from Proto-Germanic *newun, from Proto-Indo-European *h₁néwn̥. Cognate with German Low German negen, Low German negen, Dutch negen, English nine, West Frisian njoggen, Danish ni, Gothic 𐌽𐌹𐌿𐌽 (niun).

Neuntöter.et: It is not clear where the name, which appears to mean "nine-killer" (compare neun (“nine”) and töten (“to kill”)) comes from.

Neunauge.et:
From Middle High German niunouge, from Old High German niunouga (ca. 900). Equivalent to neun (“nine”) + Auge (“eye”), after the orifices near the head.
Compare Dutch negenoog, Danish niøje, Norwegian Nynorsk niauge, Swedish nejonöga. All of these are attested…

neuntältest.et: From neunte + alt, with alt put into the superlative form ältest.
